screens.title: Pointers and Arrays: Powerful Combinations
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore a foundational C concept: the tight relationship between arrays and pointers. You will see why an array name often behaves like a pointer to its first element, how pointer arithmetic moves across contiguous memory with scaling by the data type size, and why passing an array to a function actually passes a pointer. We will show concrete code examples that use array indexing, pointer arithmetic, and pointer increment to walk through elements, then demonstrate how functions can modify original arrays. Along the way we’ll highlight important differences: an array name is a constant reference to its first element and cannot be reassigned, whereas a pointer variable can. You’ll also learn the classic pitfalls: using sizeof inside a function parameter gives the pointer size, not the array size, and out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic can cause buffer overflows. By the end you’ll be able to read and write array elements using both indexing and pointer expressions, safely pass arrays to functions with an explicit length parameter, and spot common mistakes. Consider how this control over memory maps to performance and responsibility in real C programs.

screens.title: Array name decays to a pointer
screens.narratorSegment: When you declare an array like int numbers[5]; the compiler reserves a contiguous block of memory large enough to hold five integers. In most expressions the array name evaluates to a pointer to its first element. We call this decay: the name becomes a value representing the address of element zero, equivalent to taking the address explicitly with &numbers[0]. That equivalence allows you to use pointer expressions interchangeably with array indexing in many contexts. A common example is initializing a pointer: int *p = numbers; This sets p to the base address of the array. But remember a subtlety: the array name itself is not a variable you can reassign. You cannot write numbers = anotherArray; because the array identifier denotes a fixed address in memory. This is distinct from int *p which you can later reassign to point somewhere else. A useful mental model is to think of the array name as a fixed anchor at element zero. That anchor can be observed directly in code where print statements show identical values when using numbers[i] and *(numbers + i), confirming the decay in practice. Consider this when you pass arrays to functions: the parameter receives a pointer, not the whole block.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Array name decays to a pointer
What this means

An array name used in an expression becomes a pointer to the first element. This allows pointer assignment and pointer arithmetic to access array elements.

Analogy: the array name is an anchored flag at the start of a row of boxes. You can move a pointer along the boxes, but the anchored flag stays put.
Example
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int numbers[3] = {1, 2, 3};
  int *p = numbers;      // numbers decays to &numbers[0]
  printf("first = %d
", *p);
  return 0;
}
Common misconception
People expect to reassign the array name like a normal pointer. That is illegal — the identifier represents fixed storage.
Key Takeaway

Array names are anchored pointers to element zero; use pointer variables for reassignable references.

Visual: memory layout
numbers
1
2
3
Address of first box equals numbers, equivalent to &numbers[0]

screens.title: Pointer arithmetic explained
screens.narratorSegment: Pointer arithmetic is the rule set that lets you step through elements in memory by adding or subtracting integer offsets to a pointer. When you write ptr + n the compiler does not add n raw bytes; it computes ptr plus n times the size of the pointed-to type. For an int pointer on a system where sizeof(int) is four, ptr + 1 advances four bytes. That means ptr + 2 advances eight bytes, effectively pointing at the element two positions ahead. This scaling makes pointer arithmetic safe in terms of element alignment as long as you stay within bounds. A typical workflow is: compute the address with ptr + i, then dereference with *(ptr + i) to read or write that element. A misconception is to think pointer arithmetic works like raw byte arithmetic; it does not. Another subtlety: subtraction between two pointers of the same array yields a difference in element counts, not bytes. Practically, use pointer arithmetic to write tight loops or to create traversals that avoid array indexing overhead in low-level code. Always check that pointer arithmetic does not go beyond valid indices.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Pointer arithmetic
Step-by-step
1. Start with int *ptr pointing to element 0.
2. Compute ptr + i: compiler adds i * sizeof(int) to ptr.
3. Dereference *(ptr + i) to access the i-th element.
Misconception: ptr + 1 does not add one byte; it adds one element-size.
Key Takeaway

Pointer arithmetic moves in element steps. Use it consciously and keep indices bounded.

screens.title: array[i] vs *(array + i)
screens.narratorSegment: Array indexing and pointer arithmetic produce the same result when reading or writing elements: array[i] is defined as *(array + i). That means every time you index an array you are effectively doing a pointer computation and dereference. In practice, indexing is clear and idiomatic, while pointer expressions are explicit about addresses. Use pointer expressions when you already have a pointer variable or when writing generic traversal code that works with pointer parameters. For example, if a function receives int *arr you can access elements as arr[i] or *(arr + i) interchangeably. A misconception is thinking p[i] only works with arrays; it works with any pointer that points to contiguous elements. Another useful trick: pointer-style loops can increment the pointer variable directly, avoiding an index variable entirely. However, do not confuse the two forms when calculating sizes or reassigning: arr as a parameter is a pointer value, not the original declared array object. Both forms are powerful; choose the one that makes your intent clearer while maintaining bounds safety. array[i] vs *(array + i) means array[i] is shorthand for *(array + i); choose the notation that best communicates intent while keeping safety checks.. In practical terms, two notations that express the same access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › array[i] vs *(array + i)
Side-by-side example
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int a[] = {10, 20, 30};
  printf("a[1] = %d
", a[1]);
  printf("*(a + 1) = %d
", *(a + 1));
  return 0;
}
Both print the same value. Use the form that best clarifies pointer intent.
Practical note
  • When you already have a pointer, *(ptr + i) is explicit.
  • Indexing is clearer for most loops: arr[i] is idiomatic.
  • Pointer increments allow one-pass traversal without an index variable.
Check: p[i] is valid if p points into a contiguous block; it does not require the original array declaration.

screens.title: Iterating with a pointer variable
screens.narratorSegment: Pointer-based iteration moves a pointer across elements while updating the pointer itself. Start by initializing a pointer to the array base: int *cur = numbers; then read or write with *cur and advance with cur++. This pattern is useful when you want a streaming traversal or want to pass the current pointer to helper routines. Below is a small program that prints elements by incrementing a pointer. The code shows the set-up, loop condition using a length counter, dereference for output, and pointer increment. One common pitfall is using pointer increment without a length or end pointer; you must ensure the loop terminates before the pointer passes the last element. Another subtlety: if you need to use the original base address after traversal, store it separately, because the pointer will have moved. Finally, compare this style to indexed loops: both are equivalent, but pointer loops are concise when you treat the array as a stream of values. Iterating with a pointer variable means use a pointer initialized to the base, dereference to access values, and increment to move to the next element while keeping bounds checks.. In practical terms, increment a pointer to traverse an array. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Iterating with a pointer variable
Code example
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int numbers[] = {5, 10, 15, 20};
  int len = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
  int *cur = numbers;      // points to first element

  for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    printf("Element %d: %d
", i, *cur);
    cur++; // move to next element
  }
  return 0;
}
This loop uses both a counter and pointer increment to ensure safe termination and concise access.
Notes & best practices
  • Store the original base if you need to reuse it after the loop.
  • Always pair pointer increments with explicit bounds or an end pointer to avoid overruns.
  • Pointer loops are handy for streaming or when passing the moving pointer to functions.

screens.title: Passing arrays to functions
screens.narratorSegment: When you pass an array to a function in C you are passing a pointer to its first element. The callee receives a pointer value, not the full array. That keeps calls cheap for large arrays, but it means the function can modify the caller’s data. Declare the parameter as int *arr or int arr[]—both tell the compiler that the parameter is a pointer. Because the function only has a pointer, it cannot determine the original array length using sizeof. Therefore you should pass the array length as a separate parameter. This pattern is the C idiom for working with buffers: a pointer plus a length. A typical function might loop from zero to length - 1, using *(arr + i) or arr[i] to access elements, and can modify them in place. Remember the safety implication: the function must trust the caller to pass a correct length, and the caller must ensure the memory remains valid for the duration of the call. Use const qualifiers when the function should not modify elements. Passing arrays to functions means declare array parameters as int *arr or int arr[] and always pass length separately to enable safe iteration inside the function.. In practical terms, why functions receive a pointer and how to declare parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Passing arrays to functions
Parameter forms
Both declarations below are equivalent in a function parameter list because arr decays to a pointer:
void printArray(int arr[], int length);
void printArray(int *arr, int length);
Pass the length explicitly so the function can bound its loop safely.
Example: modify in-place
void doubleArrayElements(int *arr, int length) {
  for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
    *(arr + i) *= 2;
  }
}
This function modifies the caller's array directly because it operates on the same memory.

screens.title: sizeof with arrays vs pointers
screens.narratorSegment: The sizeof operator measures the size of the operand's type. In main, if you declare int numbers[5]; sizeof(numbers) yields the total bytes for all five integers because the array type is known at compile time there. But when you write a function that takes int *arr as a parameter, arr is a pointer type inside that function; sizeof(arr) returns the size of the pointer itself, typically 4 or 8 bytes depending on the architecture. This confuses learners who expect sizeof inside the function to report the original array size. That is why functions must accept a separate length parameter or use sentinel values to indicate the end. When you need the number of elements in a caller-declared array, compute it in the caller: int len = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]); then pass len along with the pointer. Remember: sizeof gives you type size, not the size of dynamically-managed memory unless you track lengths explicitly. sizeof with arrays vs pointers means use sizeof in the scope where the array type is visible; pass length to functions because parameters become pointers.. In practical terms, why sizeof(arr) in main differs from sizeof parameter inside a function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › sizeof with arrays vs pointers
Example to try
#include <stdio.h>

void f(int *arr) {
  printf("inside f: sizeof(arr) = %zu
", sizeof(arr));
}

int main() {
  int a[10];
  printf("in main: sizeof(a) = %zu
", sizeof(a));
  f(a);
  return 0;
}
The program prints different values because the function sees a pointer type.
Practical guidance
  • Compute lengths where the array's type is visible, then pass the length.
  • Do not rely on sizeof inside functions to determine array length.

screens.title: Out-of-bounds and buffer overflow
screens.narratorSegment: The most serious hazard when combining pointers and arrays is accessing memory outside the allocated bounds. If an array has N elements valid indices run from 0 to N-1. Pointer arithmetic that computes addresses before element zero or at or beyond element N points to memory you don't own. Writing through such a pointer can overwrite adjacent data, corrupt program state, or trigger security vulnerabilities like buffer overflows. Symptoms include crashes, unpredictable behavior, or exploitable conditions. To avoid this, always pair pointer operations with explicit bounds checks and pass the buffer length into functions. When iterating, stop when i equals length, not when the pointer reaches a magic address. Use defensive programming: validate inputs, avoid off-by-one errors, and prefer higher-level checks when possible. Remember that the language gives you direct memory control; that control yields power, speed, and responsibility. Treat pointer arithmetic with the same caution you would give to direct file or network operations. Out-of-bounds and buffer overflow means never dereference a pointer outside the 0..n-1 range; always validate indices and pass explicit lengths to functions.. In practical terms, why pointer arithmetic can cause crashes and vulnerabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Array name vs pointer variable
screens.narratorSegment: While array names and pointers are closely related in how you access elements, they differ in mutability. An array identifier denotes a fixed region of memory allocated for the array; you cannot assign a new address to that identifier. In contrast, a pointer variable holds an address and can be reassigned freely. For example int *p = numbers; p = anotherArray; is valid, but numbers = anotherArray; is illegal. This difference affects how you design APIs: if you want to walk a buffer and later repoint to a different buffer, use a pointer variable. If you need a named fixed-size buffer, declare an array. Another contrast is lifetime: an array declared in a function has automatic storage and its name becomes invalid once the function returns, while a pointer can reference dynamic memory whose lifetime you control. Reason about ownership and lifetime when combining arrays and pointers to avoid dangling references. This clarity helps prevent bugs where code mistakenly assumes it can reassign the original array name. You will see why an array name often behaves like a pointer to its first element, how pointer arithmetic moves across contiguous memory with scaling by the data type size, and why passing an array to a function actually passes a pointer. We will show concrete code examples that use array indexing, pointer arithmetic, and pointer increment to walk through elements, then demonstrate how functions can modify original arrays. Along the way we’ll highlight important differences: an array name is a constant reference to its first element and cannot be reassigned, whereas a pointer variable can. You’ll also learn the classic pitfalls: using sizeof inside a function parameter gives the pointer size, not the array size, and out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic can cause buffer overflows. By the end you’ll be able to read and write array elements using both indexing and pointer expressions, safely pass arrays to functions with an explicit length parameter, and spot common mistakes. Consider how this control over memory maps to performance and responsibility in real C programs.

You will demonstrate pointer arithmetic to navigate arrays, including reading and writing elements via pointer expressions. You will pass arrays to functions using pointer parameters and understand why functions receive a pointer rather than a copy of the whole array. You will also distinguish between an array name as a constant reference and a pointer variable that can be reassigned, and you will apply safety practices to prevent out-of-bounds access. Each objective is practical: for example, when you pass a large image buffer to a processing function, you pass a pointer and a length to avoid copying memory. A common misconception to watch for is assuming sizeof inside a function reports the original array size; it reports the pointer size. Keep that in mind when designing function signatures. These objectives prepare you to write efficient, safe C code that manipulates arrays directly with pointers.

These objectives translate directly into practice. You will write short programs that iterate arrays both with indexing and with pointer arithmetic, confirming values match. You will implement a function that takes an int pointer and a length, modifies elements, and returns no copy—testing that the original array changes. You will compute sizes using sizeof in main and then contrast that with sizeof inside a function to see the pointer-size behaviour. You will add boundary checks before any pointer dereference and include a length parameter to enforce safe loops. For assessment, expect multiple-choice checks that test equivalence between array indexing and pointer expressions and short coding tasks such as implementing findMax using pointer arithmetic. Practicing with these exact exercises helps you internalize both the convenience and the responsibility of direct memory control in C. By practicing, you’ll build both confidence and caution.

When you declare an array like int numbers[5]; the compiler reserves a contiguous block of memory large enough to hold five integers. In most expressions the array name evaluates to a pointer to its first element. We call this decay: the name becomes a value representing the address of element zero, equivalent to taking the address explicitly with &numbers[0]. That equivalence allows you to use pointer expressions interchangeably with array indexing in many contexts. A common example is initializing a pointer: int *p = numbers; This sets p to the base address of the array. But remember a subtlety: the array name itself is not a variable you can reassign. You cannot write numbers = anotherArray; because the array identifier denotes a fixed address in memory. This is distinct from int *p which you can later reassign to point somewhere else. A useful mental model is to think of the array name as a fixed anchor at element zero. That anchor can be observed directly in code where print statements show identical values when using numbers[i] and *(numbers + i), confirming the decay in practice. Consider this when you pass arrays to functions: the parameter receives a pointer, not the whole block.

Pointer arithmetic is the rule set that lets you step through elements in memory by adding or subtracting integer offsets to a pointer. When you write ptr + n the compiler does not add n raw bytes; it computes ptr plus n times the size of the pointed-to type. For an int pointer on a system where sizeof(int) is four, ptr + 1 advances four bytes. That means ptr + 2 advances eight bytes, effectively pointing at the element two positions ahead. This scaling makes pointer arithmetic safe in terms of element alignment as long as you stay within bounds. A typical workflow is: compute the address with ptr + i, then dereference with *(ptr + i) to read or write that element. A misconception is to think pointer arithmetic works like raw byte arithmetic; it does not. Another subtlety: subtraction between two pointers of the same array yields a difference in element counts, not bytes. Practically, use pointer arithmetic to write tight loops or to create traversals that avoid array indexing overhead in low-level code. Always check that pointer arithmetic does not go beyond valid indices.

Array indexing and pointer arithmetic produce the same result when reading or writing elements: array[i] is defined as *(array + i). That means every time you index an array you are effectively doing a pointer computation and dereference. In practice, indexing is clear and idiomatic, while pointer expressions are explicit about addresses. Use pointer expressions when you already have a pointer variable or when writing generic traversal code that works with pointer parameters. For example, if a function receives int *arr you can access elements as arr[i] or *(arr + i) interchangeably.
